state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about when you're at a T-junction in the road. The two roads meet at a right angle, just like the lines in our diagram. When you look left and right, are the angles you see always equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess the angles at a T-junction can be different, depending on how the roads are. So maybe angles \( p \) and \( q \) aren't always equal if the lines aren't parallel? But I thought alternate angles were always equal no matter what. Can you explain more about when they are equal?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about when you're sitting at a four-way intersection. The angles you see across from each other are like the vertically opposite angles in our diagram. Are those angles always equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I see what you mean about the angles at a four-way intersection being equal, like the vertically opposite angles. But I'm still confused about when alternate angles are equal. So, if the lines aren't parallel, does that mean alternate angles can be different? How do I know when they are equal?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that don't directly address the parallel lines condition for alternate angles, leading to student confusion about when alternate angles are equal, though the student does begin to question whether parallelism matters by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (T-junction roads, four-way intersections) to help the student understand abstract geometric concepts about angles, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
